title: What We Don’t Know About the Iran War
text:
P resident Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth have a ready answer to the question of how the nine-month conflict with Iran has gone: We won . But the administration has done just about everything in its power to obstruct scrutiny of that dubious claim, hiding from the public the full cost of the operation in both lives and money.

 When Senator Chris Murphy, a Democrat from Connecticut, headed to the Persian Gulf last month, he made what would once have been considered a routine request to visit Al Udeid, the giant U.S. air base outside the capital of Qatar that is home to the regional headquarters of Central Command. Typically, the base is home to 10,000 troops and more than 100 aircraft. Iran pounded it with air strikes soon after Trump launched the Iran war in February, but the conflict was largely paused when Murphy showed up.

 Murphy sits on the Senate Appropriations Committee, which must decide how the government spends taxpayer money. It’s the committee that has to sign off on expected funding requests to repair Al Udeid and other bases hit by Iranian attacks, as well as the extra $67 billion the administration has sought for war costs. Murphy requested a tour, a briefing, anything that could help him make an assessment of the damage and cost of repairs. The Pentagon said no. When Republican Senator Joni Ernst of Iowa, an Army veteran who sits on the Senate Armed Services Committee, made her own trip to the Gulf around the same time, the Defense Department told her that she would not be able to conduct base visits, a person familiar with the matter told me. Ernst’s office did not reply to a request for comment.

 Behind the rebuffs lies a decision made by Hegseth early in the war to discourage congressional travel to the region. The Pentagon couldn’t ban lawmakers from heading to the Middle East. But Hegseth instructed the Pentagon’s legislative office to “inform the appropriate congressional leadership that DoW support to congressional delegation visits will be unavailable,” according to a March 3 memo I reviewed. (DoW is an acronym for the Department of War, Hegseth’s preferred name for the Department of Defense.) To emphasize the point, the memo added: “No DoW support shall be made available for congressional travel to the USCENTCOM AOR without my approval.” (U.S. Central Command is in charge of war operations; AOR stands for “area of responsibility.”) Perhaps the edict made sense in the war’s earliest days. But the campaign had already been in limbo for many months by the time Murphy and Ernst made their requests. The policy remains in effect.

Senators aren’t the only people being denied access. Early in the war, the U.S. military provided a drumbeat of information about how the war was going. But that information was highly selective: The Defense Department offered a tally of “targets struck” (13,000 in the initial weeks) and the hardware deployed. The Pentagon regularly turned down media requests for more detail, citing “operational security.” And it has allowed only a handful of reporters to embed with troops, far fewer than in previous wars.

 Hegseth and General Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs, also held sporadic press conferences at the start of the conflict, during which Hegseth detailed how much of Iran’s military had been destroyed. The secretary insisted that the U.S. military was being transparent and that anyone who thought otherwise was trying to attack the president or was being unpatriotic. (This was after he had severely restricted media access to the Pentagon and vowed to go after purported leaks.) But as the war ground on, the press conferences stopped. Hegseth hadn’t held one since early May until last week, when he used the occasion to argue against an effort to impeach him by a congressman of his own party.

 [ Read: The last days of the Pentagon press corps ] 

 Although Congress and the public have continued to pose questions that are central to understanding the war, the administration has provided only inadequate answers.

 What exactly led to a U.S. strike on a school in Minab, Iran, on the first day of the war, killing more than 170 civilians? A targeting error was reportedly to blame, but a Centcom report on the incident has not been released, and Hegseth has never addressed the cause.

 How much damage have Iran’s strikes done to U.S. facilities in the Middle East? What little we know comes largely from photos taken by witnesses that were posted to social media, satellite images (many of them released by Iranian media), and outside estimates.

 What happened to U.S. citizens and government personnel in the region? We learned details of the hasty evacuation of military families from the giant Fifth Fleet headquarters in Bahrain only when some of the evacuees claimed , months later, that the Pentagon had treated them poorly.

 What has the war done to the supply of air-defense missiles? The Trump administration has banned some news organizations from the White House, citing their reporting on the dramatic shortfalls, among other factors.

 How many times has Iran hit U.S. bases in the region? Some significant attacks have not been disclosed, including missile strikes on the air command center at Al Udeid or on a U.S. ship in the Strait of Hormuz, both of which were later reported by the media. What were the circumstances that caused the deaths of 23 American service members and injuries to more than 850 others? And is that casualty count even accurate?

 Trump is now considering resuming strikes on Iran in an attempt to head off the reconstitution of its nuclear and missile programs, despite the strong signal of disapproval that voters sent in the midterms. Plans for a renewed escalation are on his desk, and he has told Vice President Vance not to make any overtures to Tehran, saying the time for diplomacy is over. The information vacuum of the last nine months means that even as the president contemplates taking the nation back into conflict, we have a limited picture of what has already happened.

 H egseth’s disdain for the press and for engaging with Congress began long before the war. Before his 2025 confirmation hearings, he declined to hold customary meetings with most Democratic senators on the Senate Armed Services Committee. Once in office, he barred even very senior Pentagon officials from engaging Congress without authorization.

 Pentagon officials have provided a series of classified briefings on the Iran war for lawmakers. U.S. Central Command told me that it has engaged with them roughly 60 times this year, through testimony, briefings, and phone calls. But the Pentagon’s flow of information has been restricted to partisan allies. Republican Senator Mike Rounds of South Dakota this week criticized the Pentagon for excluding Democrats from classified briefings about threats while defense officials are asking Congress for new funding. The same has happened in the House. “Pretty tough to ask all of my colleagues to support that, if they’re not even invited in to hear the information in the first place,” Rounds told Hung Cao, Trump’s nominee to lead the Navy.

 Military officials have also limited disclosures to official government watchdogs. In a September report on the costs of the war, the Congressional Budget Office—Capitol Hill’s resident bean counter—was forced to piece together information, largely from public reporting, to estimate the value of lost equipment (at least $1.9 billion, it concluded) because the Pentagon didn’t respond to its requests for information. Pentagon officials have estimated the cost of the war’s operations and replacement of munitions at about $48 billion as of mid-November, but many people believe that the full tally is far higher. Senator Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat, and several Senate colleagues complained last month that the Pentagon provided only a classified cost estimate that they were unable to share with the public. The State Department had no such qualms and disclosed its own estimate for the repair of U.S. diplomatic facilities in the region: about $184 million through the end of June.

 [ Read: How the U.S. squandered its strategic advantage ] 

 The Pentagon has said it can’t provide a cost estimate for the damage because officials haven’t decided what and where to rebuild. A spokesperson for the Pentagon declined to provide an on-the-record comment for this story.

 Murphy told me he has been trying to fill in some of the information gaps. “How on earth could we make decisions that we are empowered by the Constitution to make about whether we fund war if we can’t see it?” he said during an event last month.

 Of course, there is always an element of political grandstanding to lawmaker trips. But lawmakers have asserted their prerogative to make fact-finding missions as part of the U.S. system of checks and balances. Some congressional staff members told me they understood the Pentagon would want to avoid diverting resources during an active fight. And one former Biden administration official told me that, early in the Ukraine war, the administration at times barred lawmakers from traveling to Kyiv. But the Pentagon ultimately relaxed the ban and made security arrangements to support lawmakers’ visits, even though the Ukraine war, unlike the Iran war, is not one where the U.S. has been a direct participant.

 Robert Wilkie, who served as the Pentagon’s top legislative-affairs official during the Iraq War, told me that Hegseth’s blanket ban on access for lawmakers marked a departure from a practice that dated to at least World War II. Military leaders may not have always loved the spectacle associated with those visits, but they knew such trips were an essential part of congressional oversight. They’re also a tool the military uses to persuade lawmakers to favor bigger budgets. As Wilkie put it, referring to the gun-slinging action hero of the 20th century: “The commanders understand that it’s ‘No bucks, no Buck Rogers.’”

 T he Pentagon’s disclosures about the war’s toll on military personnel have been limited and obscured by bureaucratic choices. A Pentagon-run website lists the deaths and injuries of service members for all major U.S. conflicts going back to World War I. But in July, four deaths and dozens of injuries disappeared from its totals for Operation Epic Fury, the military’s name for the Iran war. At first, the Pentagon blamed a “data disruption” and said that there was no effort to mask the true toll. Days later, the website was updated with a new category: “Overseas Operations.” The deaths and injuries that had disappeared reemerged under the new listing. Officials pointed to a letter Trump had sent to Congress claiming that a new conflict with Iran had started on July 7.

 Some of the service members wounded in Iranian attacks have said that the military downplayed or dismissed their injuries. The Defense Department’s division of casualties into two categories makes it harder for the public to see the total toll. The Pentagon has defended the system’s accuracy despite what it has described as “website glitches.”

 [ Read: The Top Gun: Maverick theory of Pete Hegseth ] 

 Hegseth has at times appeared dismissive of casualties. A drone attack in the opening days of the war killed six troops at Port Shuaiba in Kuwait. When reporters sought details, Hegseth accused the press of hyping the loss. “When a few drones get through or tragic things happen, it’s front-page news,” he told reporters at a news conference on March 4. “The press only wants to make the president look bad.”

 Congress’s new Democratic leaders can be expected to push the Pentagon on its handling of casualties when they take over early next year. Hegseth and Trump may want to portray the war as a victory already in hand. But the defense secretary still needs lawmakers on at least one front: money. In a video statement before the planned impeachment vote, Hegseth included a pitch for the administration’s $1.5 trillion military budget request and for tens of billions more to cover the already sunk costs of the Iran war—whatever those really are.
